lesson.title: R: The Number That Makes the Ideal Gas Law Work
lesson.summary: The ideal gas constant R is the proportionality constant that connects pressure, volume, moles, and temperature in PV = nRT, and its numerical value depends entirely on which units you choose for pressure and volume.
lesson.body:
In the ideal gas law, R is what makes the equation balance no matter which gas you use or what conditions it is under. It is a true constant, meaning it does not change from one gas to another; a mole of helium and a mole of carbon dioxide obey PV = nRT with the exact same R, as long as both are behaving ideally. What R does depend on is the units you choose to measure pressure and volume in, because R is really just carrying the conversion factors needed to make the two sides of the equation match.

You can find the value of R yourself using a known set of conditions. By definition, one mole of an ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (0 degrees Celsius, which is 273 K, and 1 atm) occupies 22.4 L, a fact you will derive directly from PV = nRT in the molar volume chapter. Plugging these numbers into R = PV / (nT): R = (1 atm)(22.4 L) / (1 mol)(273 K) = 22.4 / 273. Dividing this out gives 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), which is the version of R used throughout this unit whenever pressure is given in atmospheres and volume in liters.

Because pressure can be expressed in several different units, R has several different numerical values, all describing the exact same physical constant. If you convert 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) into joules, using the fact that 1 L·atm equals 101.325 J, you get R = 0.0821 times 101.325 = 8.32 J/(mol·K), very close to the more precise value of 8.314 J/(mol·K) that you will see in SI-unit problems (the small difference comes from rounding R to three significant figures). If instead you convert into torr, using 760 torr per atm, you get R = 0.0821 times 760 = 62.4 L·torr/(mol·K). All three of these numbers, 0.0821, 8.314, and 62.4, are the same R; you simply pick whichever version matches the units given in your problem.

In practice, this means the very first step of any ideal gas law calculation is choosing which value of R to use based on the units of pressure you were given, and then making sure your volume, moles, and temperature units match. Using R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) with a pressure given in kPa, without converting first, is a guaranteed way to get a wrong answer even though every step of the algebra was correct. This unit's worked examples stick to R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) throughout, since pressures are given in atmospheres, but keep the SI version, 8.314 J/(mol·K), in mind for any problem that hands you pressure in pascals or kilopascals and volume in cubic meters or liters.
